name: Hlai
sweep_summary: hlai1239 (Hlai) is not in the catalog. The single keyword-matched bibliography item, Berlant 2008 on Grimm's law, is an Indo-European semiotics paper that Glottolog itself marks as a computerized mis-assignment from the word 'lexicons' — irrelevant, priority none.org) gives the best first-hand prominence statement — prefixal syllables pɯ/tsɯ/ɯ/kɯ are read in 轻声 (neutral, unstressed) tone before a fully toned main syllable (p. 8, fn. 1; p. 83); the book has no 重音 statement and treats Hlai as tonal and basically monosyllabic. Norquest 2016 (Brill; user-uploaded scan on archive.org) adds the historical picture: Proto-Hlai disyllables were iambic sesquisyllables with weight only on the rightmost main syllable, later monosyllabified. Lee 2026 (MDPI, 403 to our machine, read via proxy) lists eight Gei-dialect tones and is silent on stress. Not obtained: Ostapirat 2008 Routledge sketch (medium), Ouyang & Zheng 1983 survey (medium), Blagonravova 1999 Russian grammar (medium), Yuan 1994 (low). All

new_statements.quote: （2）pɯ、tsɯ、ɯ、kɯ 等几个音节作前加成分时读做轻声①（pɯ、tsɯ 两个音节声调的高低与后面一个音节声调的高低相反）。例如：pɯ˙|hweːŋ˩ 苍蝇 pɯ˙|ket˥ 蚱蜢 tsɯ˙|zoŋ˩ 脖子 tsɯ˙|jun˥ 椰子 ɯ˙|phan˩ 昨天 ɯ˙|hau˥ 明天 kɯ˙|liːu˥˧ 八哥 kɯ˙|la˥ 必须 … ① 轻声的音节仍标相近的调号，外加括号。
new_statements.translation: (2) The syllables pɯ, tsɯ, ɯ, kɯ etc., when they serve as prefixed elements, are read in neutral [unstressed] tone (for the two syllables pɯ and tsɯ the pitch height is the opposite of the pitch height of the following syllable). Examples: pɯ˙|hweːŋ˩ 'fly', pɯ˙|ket˥ 'grasshopper', tsɯ˙|zoŋ˩ 'neck', tsɯ˙|jun˥ 'coconut', ɯ˙|phan˩ 'yesterday', ɯ˙|hau˥ 'tomorrow', kɯ˙|liːu˥˧ 'myna', kɯ˙|la˥ 'must'. Footnote 1: neutral-tone syllables are still marked with the nearest tone number, in parentheses.
new_statements.citation: Ouyang Jueya 欧阳觉亚 & Zheng Yiqing 郑贻青 (1980). Líyǔ jiǎnzhì 黎语简志. Beijing: Minzu chubanshe, p. 8 (声调说明 3(2) and fn. ①); cf. p. 83.
new_statements.locator: p. 8 = PDF p. 13, chapter 一 语音, 声调 section, item 3(2) + footnote ①; also p. 83 = PDF p. 88 (prefix pɯ⁽¹⁾-, ɯ⁽³⁾- 读轻声)
new_statements.reading: Hlai (Baoding/Ha dialect as described) is a tonal, essentially monosyllabic language with no stress contrast among full syllables; the book never uses the term 重音. The only word-level prominence statement is that prefixal presyllables (pɯ-, tsɯ-, ɯ-, kɯ-) are atonic/unstressed (轻声) while the following main syllable carries full tone, i.e. prominence sits on the final (main) syllable of prefix+root words — the synchronic residue of the iambic sesquisyllabic foot Norquest 2016 (pp. 232-234) reconstructs for Proto-Hlai. For a catalog coding this would be 'no lexical stress; tonal; prefixal presyllables unstressed, main (final) syllable prominent'.

sources.citation: Norquest, Peter K. (2016 [c2015]). A Phonological Reconstruction of Proto-Hlai. Languages of Asia 13. Leiden/Boston: Brill. (Revision of the 2007 University of Arizona dissertation.)
sources.quote: As alluded to in chapter two, the PHl phonological word consisted of two types: either (a) monosyllabic or (b) disyllabic. Disyllabic words were certainly iambic, as this stress type is usually a necessary precondition in Southeast Asia for an eventual transition to a strictly monosyllabic inventory … The first hypothesis adopted here is that moraic weight became assigned exclusively to the main (rightmost) syllable, and that the first syllable in a disyllabic form lost the ability to host a mora. … I hypothesize that this loss of and subsequent lack of a mora was correlated with the steady erosion of presyllables until their eventual extinction in the Hlai daughter languages.
sources.note: Historical, not synchronic: ch. 4 (pp. 232-234) reconstructs the Pre-/Proto-Hlai phonological word as monosyllabic or disyllabic, the disyllables 'certainly iambic' sesquisyllables with moraic weight only on the rightmost main syllable; the presyllables eroded to extinction in the daughter languages (4.3.6 'Monosyllabification', p. 279). Ch. 4.2.3 (pp. 259-260) tentatively projects a PWKT stress distinction as the source of the PHl vowel-length contrast. No statement of stress placement in any modern Hlai language. sources.note: The only word-prominence statement in the book (the term 重音 'stress' never occurs; checked all 143 scanned pages): in the Baoding dialect the prefixal syllables pɯ, tsɯ, ɯ, kɯ are read in 轻声 (neutral/unstressed tone) before a fully toned main syllable, and neutral-tone syllables are transcribed with the nearest tone number in parentheses (p. 8 fn. 1). Repeated in the word-formation chapter (p. 83): pɯ⁽¹⁾-, tsɯ⁽²⁾-, ɯ⁽³⁾- prefixes 'read in neutral tone'. sources.quote: Drawing on data collected from my fieldwork, Hlai is a tonal language. The tonal system comprises eight contrastive tones, transcribed as 33, 121, 55, 11, 51, 15, 55, and 13.
sources.note: Open access at MDPI but HTTP 403 to our machine (direct and via web lookups); read once through a reader proxy, which then also went 403, so only a note is on file. Appendix A (Gei dialect, Tongshi/Wuzhishan fieldwork): 'Hlai is a tonal language. The tonal system comprises eight contrastive tones, transcribed as 33, 121, 55, 11, 51, 15, 55, and 13'; consonant and vowel inventories follow. No mention of stress or accent.
